question: The sun is highest in the sky around midday, yet on a typical day the warmest temperature arrives only in the middle of the afternoon. Why the delay?
correct_answer: Surface still gains more heat than it loses
alternative_answers: The ground takes time to heat up and warm the air
Incoming energy exceeds outgoing energy until mid-afternoon
Temperature depends on stored heat, not instant sunlight
The Earth stores heat and releases it slowly
headline_answer: Surface still gains more heat than it loses

extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Diurnal temperature variation article confirms the claimed mechanism — 'Incoming solar radiation exceeds outgoing heat energy for many hours after noon and equilibrium is usually reached from 3–5 p.m.' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diurnal_temperature_variation) — and this radiation-balance fact cannot be superseded by newer events.

explanation: Temperature reflects the total heat stored in the ground and air, not how strong the sunshine is at that instant. At noon the sun delivers energy at its fastest rate, but the ground keeps warming as long as it takes in more energy than it radiates back out. Even after noon, when the sun starts to weaken, incoming energy still outpaces outgoing heat for a few hours, so the surface and the air above it continue to warm. Only around mid-afternoon do the losses finally catch up with the gains, and that balance point is the daily maximum. It is the same reason the hottest part of summer arrives weeks after the longest day.

question: How much does a single fluffy cumulus cloud weigh: closer to 5 kilograms, 500 tonnes, or 5 million tonnes?

extra.why_interesting: Clouds look weightless, yet a single fluffy cumulus holds hundreds of tonnes of water spread over a huge volume.
extra.verification_notes: USGS Water Science School gives 500,000 kg (500 tonnes / 1.1 million lb) for a typical 1 km³ cumulus at 0.5 g/m³ water density, and the other two options are ~5 orders of magnitude off: https://www.usgs.gov/water-science-school/science/how-much-does-a-cloud-weigh

explanation: A typical cumulus cloud is about one cubic kilometre in size and holds roughly half a gram of water per cubic metre. That adds up to around 500 tonnes, the weight of about 100 elephants. It floats because that water is spread as tiny droplets across an enormous volume of air.

question: Which is hotter: the surface of the Sun or a bolt of lightning?

extra.why_interesting: Most people assume nothing on Earth beats the Sun for heat, but a lightning channel is roughly five times hotter than the Sun's surface.
extra.verification_notes: Lightning's return-stroke channel exceeds 27,800 °C (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning) versus the Sun's photosphere at ~5,772 K (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosphere), so lightning is ~5x hotter; 'surface' correctly excludes the million-degree corona.

explanation: A lightning channel briefly reaches around 30,000 degrees Celsius, while the Sun's visible surface is only about 5,500 degrees. The Sun's core is far hotter, but its surface loses to a summer thunderstorm.

question: A desert is defined by how little precipitation falls, not by heat. By that rule, what is the largest desert on Earth?

extra.why_interesting: Deserts are defined by lack of precipitation, not heat, so the largest one is the coldest place on Earth.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's List of deserts by area ranks the Antarctic Desert #1 at 14,200,000 km² (vs Arctic 13.9M, Sahara 9.2M), and Antarctica's ~150 mm/yr precipitation is well under the 250 mm desert threshold; the question's 'not by heat' clause correctly forecloses the Sahara. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deserts_by_area

explanation: Antarctica receives only about 50 millimetres of precipitation a year in its interior, less than the Sahara. At roughly 14 million square kilometres it is far bigger than the Sahara, making it the largest desert on the planet.

question: True or false: if the air gets cold enough, it becomes physically impossible for snow to fall.

extra.why_interesting: The phrase 'too cold to snow' is repeated every winter, yet it is a myth. Snow can fall at any temperature below freezing if there is moisture.
extra.verification_notes: NSIDC states 'While it can be too warm to snow, it cannot be too cold to snow' and NWS says 'It's never too cold for snow, but perhaps too dry' (https://nsidc.org/learn/parts-cryosphere/snow/science-snow), confirming the claimed answer of False.

explanation: False. Snow can fall at any temperature below freezing, and it has been recorded at minus 40 degrees and colder. Very cold air holds much less moisture, so heavy snowfalls become rare, but there is no temperature at which snow becomes impossible.

question: In 1816, Europe and North America suffered the 'Year Without a Summer', with snow falling in June and crops failing. The eruption of which Indonesian volcano the year before was to blame?

extra.why_interesting: A volcano on the other side of the world caused summer snow in Europe and famine, and even helped inspire Frankenstein.
extra.verification_notes: Mount Tambora (Sumbawa, Indonesia) erupted April 1815 and is the established primary cause of the 1816 Year Without a Summer, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_Without_a_Summer

explanation: Tambora erupted in April 1815 in the largest volcanic eruption in recorded history. Its ash and sulphur dimmed sunlight worldwide and dropped global temperatures the following year. The gloomy, rainy summer of 1816 kept Mary Shelley indoors in Switzerland, where she began writing Frankenstein.

question: How fast does a large raindrop hit the ground: closer to walking speed, sprinting speed, or highway driving speed?

extra.why_interesting: Raindrops feel fast when they hit your face, but air resistance caps them at roughly the speed of a sprinter.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Rain article gives large 5 mm drops an impact speed of ~9 m/s (20 mph), which matches sprinting speed rather than walking (~3 mph) or highway driving (~65 mph): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain

explanation: Air resistance limits large raindrops to a terminal velocity of about 9 metres per second, roughly 32 kilometres per hour. That is about the speed of a good sprinter. Drizzle falls far more slowly, and no raindrop ever reaches highway speed.

question: Name the Pacific climate pattern that Peruvian fishermen named after the baby Jesus, because its warm waters tended to arrive around Christmas.

extra.why_interesting: A world-changing climate pattern got its name from a Christmas timing quirk noticed by fishermen.
extra.verification_notes: NOAA Climate.gov and PMEL confirm Peruvian fishermen named the warm coastal current 'El Niño' after the Christ Child for its Christmastime arrival; the etymology is historical and cannot be made stale (https://www.climate.gov/news-features/blogs/enso/what-el-ni%C3%B1o%E2%80%93southern-oscillation-enso-nutshell).

explanation: El Niño is Spanish for 'the boy' and refers to the Christ child. Fishermen off Peru noticed the unusually warm current appearing in late December. The pattern warms the eastern Pacific every few years and shifts rainfall, droughts and storms across the globe. Its cool opposite is called La Niña.

question: Count the seconds between a lightning flash and its thunder, then divide by three. What does the result tell you?
correct_answer: Distance to the lightning in kilometres
alternative_answers: how far away the lightning is
how many kilometres away the storm is

extra.why_interesting: A folk trick everyone has heard turns out to be real physics: sound takes about three seconds per kilometre.
extra.verification_notes: Sound travels ~1 km per 3 seconds, so dividing the flash-to-bang delay by three gives the distance to the strike in kilometres, as stated in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunder; the fact is a physical constant and cannot be superseded.

explanation: Light reaches you almost instantly, but sound travels at about 340 metres per second, so it needs roughly three seconds to cover one kilometre. Dividing the delay by three gives the distance to the strike in kilometres. Dividing by five gives it in miles.

question: One lake in Venezuela sees lightning storms on about 260 nights a year, more than anywhere else on Earth. Name it.

extra.why_interesting: One lake sees lightning on around 260 nights a year, a storm so reliable that sailors once used it as a lighthouse.
extra.verification_notes: Lake Maracaibo is confirmed as Earth's top lightning hotspot by NASA/Albrecht et al. 2016 (https://ghrc.nsstc.nasa.gov/pub/lis/climatology/LIS/doc/Where_are_the_lightning_hotspots_on_Earth.pdf) and Guinness, with nothing superseding it as of 2026; the '260 nights' detail is looser than authoritative figures (~297 nights) but doesn't make the answer ambiguous or wrong.

explanation: Warm, humid air from the Caribbean is trapped by the Andes around Lake Maracaibo, feeding thunderstorms almost every night. The Catatumbo lightning, named after the river that feeds the lake, produces more lightning flashes per square kilometre than any other place on the planet and could once be seen by ships hundreds of kilometres away.
